Certains quittent leur demeure pour accomplir un engagement dont l'origine remonte à plusieurs siècles, tandis que d'autres entreprennent un voyage afin de trouver un maître capable de leur enseigner une discipline nouvelle. Un jeune Elfe peut rechercher l'aventure par goût des terres inconnues, alors qu'un ancien souhaite retrouver un lieu associé à des souvenirs personnels dont il désire comprendre les transformations.

Les relations familiales constituent également une source importante d'interprétation. Un personnage peut avoir grandi parmi des proches qui ont connu personnellement les grandes guerres des anciens temps et considérer leurs décisions avec respect, sans partager nécessairement toutes leurs convictions. Il peut souhaiter poursuivre l'œuvre d'un parent, préserver une demeure ou accomplir une promesse faite avant sa naissance. Les départs vers l'Ouest peuvent également modifier profondément les relations entre membres d'une même famille, particulièrement lorsque certains souhaitent demeurer en Terre du Milieu tandis que d'autres estiment leur temps achevé. Un personnage peut ainsi consacrer une partie de son existence à préparer son propre départ, tout en conservant des engagements dont l'accomplissement le retient encore dans les terres mortelles.

Le rapport au temps doit influencer les décisions du personnage sans lui imposer une lenteur permanente. Un Elfe peut se montrer patient lorsqu'il entreprend une œuvre destinée à durer plusieurs siècles, puis agir avec une grande rapidité lorsqu'il estime qu'une situation exige une décision immédiate. Sa longévité peut nourrir la prudence, mais également l'audace lorsque son expérience lui permet de reconnaître une occasion particulière. Elle peut favoriser la compréhension des conséquences lointaines, tout en lui donnant parfois des difficultés à mesurer l'urgence des préoccupations humaines. Un personnage peut apprendre à respecter les décisions de ses compagnons mortels, même lorsqu'elles paraissent précipitées à ses yeux, particulièrement lorsqu'il comprend que leur existence leur laisse moins de temps pour accomplir leurs projets.

La mémoire peut fournir des motivations plus profondes. Un Elfe peut conserver le souvenir d'une cité détruite et chercher à retrouver les ouvrages qui en furent sauvés, tandis qu'un autre souhaite établir les circonstances exactes d'un événement dont les récits transmis par les survivants demeurent contradictoires. Un personnage peut également porter la responsabilité d'une décision ancienne, particulièrement lorsqu'il estime avoir contribué à une guerre ou à la destruction d'une communauté. Il peut chercher à réparer les conséquences de ses actes, protéger les descendants de ceux qu'il n'a pas su sauver ou préserver les connaissances dont la perte compromettrait la mémoire de son peuple. Ces engagements donnent à l'aventure une portée qui dépasse parfois les événements immédiats, sans empêcher le personnage de développer de nouvelles amitiés et de trouver des raisons personnelles de poursuivre son voyage.

Les relations avec les autres peuples offrent de nombreuses possibilités d'évolution. Un Elfe habitué aux traditions de l'Ouest peut découvrir auprès d'un Nain une conception de l'art fondée sur des connaissances qu'il ne possède pas, tandis qu'un personnage méfiant envers les Hommes peut apprendre à apprécier leur courage et leur capacité à accomplir de grandes œuvres au cours d'une existence brève. Les Hobbits peuvent lui révéler la valeur d'une vie consacrée aux relations familiales et aux occupations ordinaires, particulièrement lorsqu'il a longtemps vécu parmi des communautés préoccupées par les anciennes guerres et les grandes entreprises. Ces rencontres peuvent modifier ses convictions, l'amener à remettre en cause certains préjugés ou renforcer des fidélités dont il comprend désormais mieux la valeur.

Les professions accessibles aux Quendi reflètent la diversité de leurs traditions et de leurs connaissances. Un Guerrier peut avoir reçu une formation dans les forces chargées de défendre une cité ou parmi les compagnies engagées dans les guerres anciennes, tandis qu'un Rôdeur peut posséder une connaissance approfondie des terres sauvages, des animaux et des passages fréquentés par les voyageurs. Un Roublard peut avoir développé ses compétences au cours de missions discrètes, de voyages ou de négociations exigeant une grande prudence, alors qu'un Barde peut consacrer son existence à la conservation des récits, à l'étude des langues et aux traditions musicales de son peuple. D'autres Professions peuvent être envisagées selon la Culture choisie et les compatibilités prévues par MERP-UI. L'accès aux disciplines magiques demeure soumis aux enseignements et aux restrictions définis par le système RMU, sans que les dons naturels des Quendi ou leur longévité accordent automatiquement la maîtrise des sorts.

Le choix de l'Âge constitue enfin un élément déterminant. Au Premier Âge, un personnage peut appartenir aux grandes communautés du Beleriand, participer aux migrations et aux guerres ou vivre parmi les peuples demeurés dans les régions orientales. Au Deuxième Âge, il peut connaître la prospérité des établissements du Lindon et d'Eregion, les échanges avec les Khazâd ou les guerres contre Sauron. Au Troisième Âge, il peut appartenir aux communautés de Fondcombe, de la Lórien, du Lindon ou des royaumes sylvains, tandis que le Quatrième Âge lui offre la possibilité de poursuivre son existence dans une Terre du Milieu où les Hommes occupent désormais une place prépondérante. Chaque époque donne une signification différente à son ascendance, aux événements dont il conserve personnellement le souvenir et aux raisons qui peuvent le conduire à entreprendre un voyage.

La Race Elfes — Quendi est disponible dans MERP-UI durant les quatre Âges de la Terre du Milieu, sous réserve des circonstances historiques propres à chaque période. Elle représente les qualités fondamentales communes aux Premiers-Nés : leur existence liée à Arda, leurs sens remarquables, leur endurance, leur légèreté de mouvement et leur nature préservée du vieillissement humain. Le choix d'une Culture précise ensuite l'origine du personnage, sa parenté, son éducation, ses langues, ses traditions et les compétences qu'il a acquises. Les Vanyar, Noldor, Teleri, Sindar, Nandor, Elfes sylvains, Avari et les autres communautés développées dans MERP possèdent des histoires particulières qui influencent leurs relations et leurs possibilités professionnelles. Certaines origines exigent une justification spécifique selon l'Âge choisi, particulièrement lorsque le personnage appartient à un peuple établi principalement en Aman.

Les unions exceptionnelles entre Elfes et Hommes, ainsi que leurs descendants, les Peredhil, sont représentées séparément parmi les Races restreintes de MERP-UI et relèvent de conditions particulières de création. Leur histoire, les choix qui peuvent leur être accordés et les conséquences de leur ascendance mixte doivent donc être distingués de la condition propre aux Quendi.

Avant de valider la création d'un personnage elfique, le joueur et le Meneur devraient déterminer son peuple d'origine, sa famille, la demeure où il a grandi et les disciplines auxquelles il a consacré son existence. Ils devraient également préciser son âge, les événements qu'il a personnellement connus et ceux qu'il connaît seulement par les récits de sa communauté. Ses relations avec les autres peuples, son attitude envers les anciennes traditions et son éventuel désir de rejoindre l'Ouest contribuent à définir sa personnalité, mais ses motivations doivent également lui appartenir. Il peut souhaiter préserver une demeure, retrouver un savoir, accomplir une promesse, réparer une faute ou découvrir des terres que ses ancêtres n'ont jamais parcourues. Les événements de son aventure lui permettront de confronter ces aspirations aux engagements reçus et de décider de ce qu'il souhaite encore accomplir en Terre du Milieu.

Un Elfe possède une existence dont la durée dépasse celle des royaumes et des générations humaines. Il peut conserver le souvenir des terres disparues, poursuivre des œuvres entreprises depuis des siècles et demeurer fidèle à des compagnons dont les descendants ont oublié le nom. Cette mémoire lui offre des connaissances et des responsabilités particulières, mais les circonstances de son existence lui permettent également de découvrir, d'apprendre et de choisir des voies nouvelles. Les liens qu'il décidera de préserver, les œuvres auxquelles il consacrera son temps et les engagements qu'il acceptera détermineront la place qu'il occupera parmi les Quendi.

Elves — The Quendi

In a dwelling in Lindon, a craftsman examines a harp whose tuning peg has split. The instrument belongs to a family he has known for many generations. He remembers its first owner, the songs he composed, and the celebration at which the harp was given to his daughter. He selects a piece of wood preserved in his workshop, carefully fits the replacement, and tunes the strings before returning the instrument. Its owner then asks whether he still remembers the melody her father used to play when she was a child. The craftsman sets down his tools, takes up the harp, and sounds a few notes whose sequence he has not heard for several centuries. For a while, they remain listening to the song they both know, before speaking of the companions who once shared it with them. His work complete, he returns to a piece begun several years earlier, whose ornaments he has yet to fashion. He wishes to finish it before the next gathering of his family, but will gladly devote a few more days to a part whose proportions do not yet satisfy him.

Several hundred leagues away, beneath the trees of Greenwood the Great, a young Elf accompanies a patrol charged with watching the paths used by travellers. She recognises the tracks of a wild boar, notices a recently broken branch, and pauses to listen to movements reaching her through the foliage. She has known the paths of this forest since childhood, but knows nothing of the western cities sometimes mentioned by the elders of her people. The tales of Beleriand and the great Elven kingdoms seem as distant to her as the legends of Men, although some of those who recount them actually lived in those days. When the leader of the patrol discovers marks left by several strangers beside a stream, he asks her to examine the banks and identify where they crossed. She finds their tracks, but also notices that one of the travellers was limping and another carried an unusually heavy burden. These observations lead the guards to change their route so that they may find the group before it enters a dangerous part of the forest. The young Elf thus continues her apprenticeship among more experienced companions, some of whom have watched these paths for several centuries.

At the Grey Havens, a mariner watches the preparations of a ship bound for the West. He knows every part of its hull, the qualities of the timber used in its construction, and the members of its crew, several of whom have already undertaken long voyages. A family arrived the previous evening, bringing a few chests, instruments, and the books they wish to take with them. Among them is an Elf-woman he once knew in Beleriand, before the wars destroyed their common home. They speak of friends who are gone and of the years that have passed since their last meeting, and she then asks whether he finally intends to make the crossing himself. He replies that other ships must still be prepared and that several families have announced their arrival in the seasons ahead. He has devoted much of his existence to guiding his people towards the western lands, yet he still has companions and responsibilities in the Havens to which he remains deeply attached.

All belong to the Quendi, the Firstborn of Ilúvatar. Their existence may extend across the Ages of the world, yet their experiences, knowledge, and aspirations remain profoundly different. Some have beheld the light of the Two Trees and known the great lords of ancient days; others were born long after the destruction of their kingdoms, within communities where the events of the First Age are known only through the tales of the elders. Some live in dwellings that preserve the arts of the Eldar, while others inhabit forests, secluded valleys, or settlements whose very existence is unknown to Men. All share a nature intimately bound to the fate of Arda, remarkable faculties, and a memory that lends particular depth to their commitments. Their history is that of a people who learned to love the world, to understand its works, and to preserve what they hold dear, while discovering over the centuries that the kingdoms, peoples, and places to which they remain attached are destined to change.

The Firstborn Beneath the Stars

The Elves awoke upon the shores of Cuiviénen, far away in the eastern lands of Middle-earth, before the Sun and Moon had begun to illuminate the skies of Arda. The stars were the first lights they beheld, and their memory remained deeply woven into the traditions of their people. They called themselves Quendi, Those Who Speak, for speech enabled them to give form to their thoughts and name the beings and things they discovered. The earliest days of their existence were devoted to exploring the surrounding lands, learning language, and forming the first communities. They wandered along the shores of the lake, discovered the forests, observed the animals, and began to recognise the properties of plants and materials. Relationships between the earliest groups encouraged the development of languages, while songs accompanied their gatherings, their work, and the passing down of memories. This gradual discovery of the world held a fundamental place in their history, for the Quendi learned to know Arda at a time when the kingdoms of Men did not yet exist and much of the land remained untouched by civilisation.

Yet those first centuries also brought fear. Morgoth had learned of the awakening of the Children of Ilúvatar and sought to extend his influence over them, sending his servants into the regions where they dwelt. The Quendi were confronted with disappearances, dangers whose origins they did not understand, and lies intended to turn them against the Powers of the West. They did not yet know the Valar, whose existence was revealed to them only when Oromë discovered them during his travels. At first, the encounter was marked by apprehension, for some Elves had learned to fear horsemen travelling through the surrounding lands. Oromë gradually won their trust and carried news of their awakening to Valinor, where the Valar decided to invite them to come to Aman. This invitation promised the Quendi the protection of the Powers and the possibility of dwelling in lands preserved from Morgoth's dominion, but it also required them to leave the places where they had been born and the communities they had begun to establish.

The decision to follow Oromë marked one of the deepest divisions in their history. Some Quendi accepted the invitation and undertook the Great Journey westward, becoming the Eldar, while others preferred to remain in their ancestral lands or continue their own existence in Middle-earth. The latter received the name Avari, the Unwilling. The Eldar crossed immense regions, encountered obstacles, and experienced further separations when certain communities decided to halt their journey. Their travels lasted many years, and successive generations were able to develop particular traditions through their contact with the lands they occupied. The Avari, meanwhile, continued their history in the eastern regions, where their descendants formed peoples of whose existence the western chronicles preserve only a small part. These ancient choices do not represent a moral division among the Quendi, but bear witness to their different experiences and the relationships they chose to maintain with the Valar and the lands of their birth.

The Elves who beheld the light of the Two Trees in Aman were called the Calaquendi, the Elves of the Light, while those who never saw it were known as the Moriquendi, the Elves of Darkness. This distinction holds an important place in ancient traditions, particularly among peoples who attach great value to the knowledge acquired in the presence of the Valar. It must not, however, be understood as a fundamental difference of nature, nor as a division between good and evil. A Sinda who remained in Beleriand may possess remarkable wisdom and knowledge without ever having beheld the Two Trees, while a Noldo who returned from Aman may commit errors whose consequences endure across several Ages. All belong to the Quendi, and their common origin forms the foundation of their Race. The languages, customs, and knowledge that distinguish them belong to the Cultures developed throughout their history.

The Great Kindreds of the Quendi

Among the Eldar, three great kindreds emerged: the Vanyar, the Noldor, and the Teleri, whose traditions took different forms during the Great Journey and after their settlement in the western lands. The Vanyar reached Aman and remained close to the Valar, developing a way of life deeply connected with the teachings of the Powers and the traditions of the Eldar who had beheld the Two Trees. Their presence in Middle-earth was exceptional during the following Ages, particularly after the return of the Noldor to Beleriand. Their history and customs are therefore chiefly associated with Aman, where their communities retain a particular place among the Elven peoples. A character belonging to the Vanyar possesses a distinguished heritage, but any presence in Middle-earth requires a historical explanation appropriate to the period of the campaign.

The Noldor developed in Aman a remarkable civilisation, distinguished by the extent of its knowledge and the quality of its works. They studied languages, history, and the properties of matter, perfecting arts whose achievements would profoundly shape the Ages that followed. Their smiths, jewellers, and master craftsmen attained exceptional skill, encouraged by the instruction received from the Valar, particularly Aulë. This pursuit of knowledge was accompanied by great curiosity, but could also nourish rivalry and pride. The events surrounding the Silmarils and the oath of Fëanor led a large part of the Noldor to leave Aman and return to Middle-earth, where they founded kingdoms and took part in the long wars against Morgoth. The descendants of these communities preserved their attachment to ancient knowledge, but their history was permanently marked by the consequences of the oaths, divisions, and wars that brought about the destruction of their settlements.

The Teleri experienced a more complex history, for their progress westward was marked by several separations. Some eventually reached Aman, where they developed traditions particularly associated with the sea, navigation, and the arts of song. Others halted their journey and remained in Middle-earth, gradually forming peoples whose languages and customs evolved along different paths. The Sindar, notably associated with the kingdom of Doriath and the settlements of Beleriand, developed a remarkable civilisation under the rule of Thingol and Melian. Their traditions gave great importance to music, architecture, the arts, and knowledge of the lands they inhabited. The Nandor, who had abandoned the Great Journey, followed other paths and settled in different regions, where their descendants contributed to the formation of the woodland Elven communities. The Silvan Elves thus inherited traditions developed among forests, rivers, and communities whose history often remained far removed from the great kingdoms of the West.

The Avari occupy a particular place within this diversity. Their ancestors refused Oromë's invitation and continued their existence in the eastern lands, where they developed traditions of which the western Eldar possess only fragmentary knowledge. Their settlements, languages, and relationships with other peoples evolved over centuries about which the western chronicles record few events. Some groups may have maintained exchanges with other Elven or human communities, while others remained far from the great roads and known kingdoms. Their history cannot be reduced to the single decision made by their ancestors, for later generations also had to face migrations, wars, and the transformation of the territories they occupied. The developments of MERP make it possible to explore these peoples and their descendants, particularly through certain Cultures such as the Penni, whose distinctive features extend the information left by Tolkien.

These differences between the great kindreds help explain the richness of Elven Cultures in MERP-UI. A Noldo raised among craftsmen may know the traditions of smithcraft and the ancient languages, while a Silvan Elf possesses extensive experience of his woodland territory. A Sinda from an ancient lineage may preserve the memory of vanished kingdoms, whereas an Avar from the eastern regions belongs to a community whose customs are almost unknown to his companions. Such knowledge and traditions result from a particular education and must remain distinct from the fundamental characteristics shared by all Quendi as members of the same Race.

An Existence Bound to the Fate of Arda

Elves do not age as Men do. Their bodies reach maturity and then retain a relatively stable appearance for centuries, sometimes millennia. They do not die of old age and are naturally spared many diseases that afflict mortal peoples. Their existence nevertheless remains exposed to wounds, violence, and suffering capable of destroying their bodies or causing them to relinquish life. The wars of ancient Ages claimed the lives of countless Quendi, some of whom were already centuries old when they fell in battle. Their longevity therefore grants them no invulnerability, but profoundly transforms the way they regard danger, commitments, and the consequences of their actions.

The essential difference between the Quendi and Men concerns the fate of their spirits. When an Elf dies, his fëa remains bound to Arda and is summoned to the Halls of Mandos, where it may find rest and, according to the individual's history and the judgements concerning his fate, receive a body once more. Men, by contrast, depart beyond the bounds of the world after death, following a destiny that even the Elves cannot fully understand. This distinction lends particular depth to relationships between the two peoples, especially when friendships or unions bring them together. An Elf may remain in Middle-earth long after the passing of human companions whom he knew and loved, personally preserving their words and the events of their lives when even their descendants have forgotten their names.

This permanence also transforms the way the Quendi pursue their undertakings. A work interrupted may be resumed several centuries later, knowledge preserved by a master may be passed on to many generations of pupils, and an ancient promise may continue to bind the one who made it. Some Elves witnessed the founding of cities whose remains Men now consider ancient ruins. They have watched forests grow, borders shift, and kingdoms vanish whose sovereigns were once their companions. Their personal memories thus connect events that other peoples know only through accounts, but such continuity may become painful when the places they love are transformed beyond recognition.

Yet the existence of the Quendi remains bound to the fate of Arda, and their sojourn in Middle-earth possesses limits of its own. As the Ages pass, the power of their spirit over their body increases, and those who remain indefinitely in the mortal lands are gradually exposed to the fading of their physical presence. Elven traditions associate this phenomenon with the decline of their people and the transformation of the world, particularly as the ancient powers that helped preserve certain kingdoms lose their influence. Many thus experience, sooner or later, a longing to reach Aman, where their existence may continue under different conditions. Others remain attached to the places of their birth, the communities they protect, or the works they still wish to accomplish. This decision becomes particularly important as the Third Age draws to its close and the dominion of Men begins.

A Nature of Remarkable Refinement

Elves resemble Men in their general shape and proportions, but their appearance often possesses a singular harmony and lightness. They are usually tall, slender, and well proportioned, with supple movements that reveal remarkable coordination. Their faces long retain the features of maturity without displaying the ordinary marks of human ageing, while their bodily hair is generally sparse. Most male Elves are beardless, although rare exceptions exist among the eldest. These characteristics nevertheless vary according to lineage and individual, so that no single physical description could adequately represent all the Quendi. Hair may range from deep black through shades of brown to silver or gold, while eyes display a wide variety of colours and expressions.

Traditions sometimes associate particular features with certain kindreds. The Vanyar are especially renowned for their golden hair, while the Noldor are frequently described as dark-haired, although their great families possess notable exceptions. The different peoples descended from the Teleri display comparable diversity, enriched over generations by migrations and unions between communities. Such differences determine neither personal qualities nor knowledge, but may help recall an individual's ancestry or family traditions. Clothing, jewellery, and the objects carried also play an important role in how the Quendi present themselves, particularly when certain ornaments possess family significance or recall an ancient affiliation.

Their constitution combines endurance with great physical grace. Elves can travel long distances, sustain prolonged exertion, and move confidently across difficult terrain. Their balance and precision allow them to overcome obstacles with remarkable lightness, while their steps sometimes leave shallower traces than those of other peoples. The tales speak, in particular, of Elves able to walk upon fresh snow without sinking into it as Men would. Such an aptitude does not, however, make every Quendi an accomplished hunter or acrobat. A scholar who has devoted several centuries to studying languages retains the natural qualities of his Race without necessarily possessing the experience of a Silvan scout, while a craftsman accustomed to workshops must learn the techniques of mountain travel before he can move with the assurance of an experienced guide.

The senses of the Quendi are particularly keen. Their sight allows them to distinguish details at great distances, perceive slight movements, and retain excellent vision beneath the light of stars or the Moon. Absolute darkness nevertheless remains a genuine obstacle, for their natural faculties do not constitute magical vision capable of piercing every shadow. Their hearing is equally remarkable, particularly when recognising a familiar voice, distinguishing the subtleties of a song, or noticing a slight change in the sounds of a forest. Experience then teaches them how to interpret these perceptions. An inhabitant of Lindon may recognise the tuning of an ancient instrument without knowing how to identify an animal's tracks, while a Silvan hunter possesses extensive knowledge of the movements and sounds of his territory without necessarily mastering the musical arts of his western kindred.

Their relationship with rest also differs from that of Men. Elves may find a form of repose in waking contemplation, during which their minds wander through memories or linger upon thoughts without remaining entirely subject to the immediate demands of their surroundings. They also know sleep, particularly when circumstances or fatigue require it, but their habits allow them to maintain long watches and organise their lives according to a rhythm less closely bound to the alternation of day and night. These qualities favour prolonged journeys, vigilance, and certain activities demanding sustained attention, without removing the need to preserve their strength. Their capacity for recovery remains remarkable, but it does not protect them from exhaustion or the consequences of serious wounds.

Families, Unions, and Childhood Among the Quendi

Family holds an important place in the lives of Elves, although their longevity and the relative rarity of births give it characteristics very different from those of human societies. Unions are generally regarded as enduring commitments, binding those who enter them profoundly, since marital bonds belong to an existence that may continue throughout the Ages of the world. Families preserve the memory of their ancestors and the relationships connecting them with other lineages, particularly when several members took part in founding a city or in the defining events of their people. Descendants may personally know very ancient relatives whose memories reach back to times the younger generations have never experienced. This closeness encourages the transmission of knowledge, but may also create considerable expectations when children belong to houses whose members have long exercised political, military, or scholarly responsibilities.

Elven children are relatively few, and their birth constitutes a major event in the life of a family. Their growth follows the rhythm particular to the Quendi, while their education extends over many years, during which parents, relatives, and masters gradually pass on the knowledge and customs of their community. The young learn to recognise the places of their home, the people to whom they are related, and the traditions governing relationships between families. Games, songs, and stories contribute to their learning, particularly by helping them discover the languages, animals, and plants of their surroundings. In woodland communities, children gradually accompany adults on journeys and in the work necessary for communal life, while those growing up in a city frequent workshops, gardens, and the places where masters share their knowledge.

Their apprenticeship may then follow very different paths. A young Noldo may discover the properties of stones and metals under a master craftsman, while a Silvan Elf learns to recognise signs left by animals and the changing seasons. A girl raised in a dwelling in Lindon may receive musical instruction from a relative whose compositions date back several centuries, whereas a young Sinda discovers the architectural traditions of his people by accompanying the masters responsible for maintaining buildings. The natural aptitudes of the Quendi favour such learning, but their long lives do not immediately grant them mastery of their chosen disciplines. Movements require practice, languages careful study, and responsibilities experience that even the elders themselves had to acquire in their youth.

Relationships between generations possess particular depth. A child may receive instruction from a grandparent who personally knew the kingdoms whose tales he hears, while a master may successively teach pupils belonging to several branches of the same family. This continuity makes it possible to preserve traditions with remarkable precision, but may also provoke disagreements when younger Elves wish to travel or develop arts different from those cultivated by their relatives. A character may deeply admire his parents while believing that their attachment to an ancient dwelling limits the opportunities open to him. Conversely, a young Elf may choose to devote his life to preserving the works of a family whose members have departed for the West, considering their protection a responsibility he willingly accepts.

Wars and catastrophes have profoundly affected these relationships. The loss of a family member may leave a lasting absence within a community whose inhabitants shared that individual's life for several centuries. A craftsman who perishes takes with him experience and memories that his pupils may pass on, but which they will never possess in their entirety. Families separated by migrations or departures to Aman may also remain apart for long periods, particularly when their members have chosen different destinies. Yet these losses do not condemn the survivors to an existence devoted solely to the past. Some continue raising their children, form new friendships, and devote their efforts to works intended to benefit future generations.

Elven Dwellings and Daily Life

The communities of the Quendi inhabit settlements whose organisation depends closely upon their history and the resources of their territory. Some live in great stone dwellings, ancient cities, or sheltered valleys, where works completed over centuries bear witness to the quality of Elven craftsmanship. Others inhabit woodland communities, timber houses, or more modest settlements whose buildings are adapted to the trees, waterways, and surrounding terrain. Architectural choices reflect the knowledge and preferences of each people, but also the circumstances in which their dwellings were founded. A city built to accommodate the court of a sovereign possesses meeting halls, places of reception, and specialised workshops, while a Silvan community may favour scattered dwellings connected by paths known to the inhabitants and protected through their intimate knowledge of the forest.

Maintaining these settlements requires numerous activities, of which accounts of the great wars preserve only a small part. Elves cultivate gardens, tend orchards, gather the resources of the forests, and prepare the food necessary for their subsistence. Woodworkers fashion furniture, instruments, and equipment used within their homes, while weavers make clothing suited to the seasons and activities of their communities. Some devote themselves to animal husbandry, navigation, trade, or watching the surrounding territories. Those responsible for stores ensure that sufficient resources are preserved for difficult periods, particularly in settlements exposed to warfare or the dangers of neighbouring regions. Such occupations give the Quendi a daily existence as varied as that of other peoples, even when the quality of their works bears witness to experience accumulated over several centuries.

Gardens and cultivated spaces occupy an important place in many Elven communities. The inhabitants know the plants they tend, the needs of trees, and the changes brought by the seasons. A gardener may care for an orchard whose first trees were planted by his ancestors, follow the growth of saplings over several decades, and choose the species best suited to the soil and light. Woodland communities possess particularly extensive knowledge of the resources offered by their surroundings, while the inhabitants of sheltered valleys may arrange their lands to ensure the preservation of gardens and cultivated areas. Such practices require regular labour, observation, and attention to natural transformations, particularly when the inhabitants wish to preserve the qualities of their territory for many years.

Domestic objects likewise reveal the care devoted to craftsmanship. A table, garment, instrument, or simple utensil may be fashioned to last many years, then repaired and passed on to other members of the community. Craftsmen choose their materials according to their properties and seek to create objects that are useful, durable, and pleasant to handle. This pursuit of quality concerns prestigious works as much as ordinary necessities. Elves need baskets, ropes, shoes, tools, and vessels, whose manufacture does not necessarily constitute an extraordinary art. Their long experience nevertheless allows some masters to attain remarkable precision, particularly when they perfect the same techniques over several centuries.

Shared meals, celebrations, songs, and gatherings hold an important place in the lives of the Quendi. Communities celebrate the seasons, unions, reunions, and significant events in their history, sometimes bringing together families separated for many years. Assemblies provide opportunities to make decisions concerning work, exchanges, or the protection of the territory, while evening gatherings allow ancient tales and compositions to be passed on. Some participants personally know the figures celebrated in the songs, lending these occasions a particular depth. Joy, friendship, laughter, and ordinary activities belong fully to Elven existence, whose long duration provides many opportunities to cultivate personal relationships without removing disagreements or rivalries.

Trades, Arts, and Knowledge

Over the Ages, the Quendi have developed craft and scholarly traditions of remarkable richness. Their longevity allows them to devote many years to studying a discipline, perfecting the techniques received from their masters, and undertaking works whose completion requires exceptional patience. Craftsmen attach great importance to the properties of materials, the harmony of proportions, and the relationship between an object and its intended purpose. A master carpenter may study the form of a tree for a long time before choosing the timber needed to construct an instrument, while a stonemason examines the natural lines of a block to determine how it may best be used. Such attention encourages remarkable achievements, but always results from thorough work and knowledge passed down through generations.

The Noldor are especially renowned for their mastery of metals, precious stones, and scholarly disciplines. The works of their masters reveal exceptional knowledge of matter, enriched by the instruction received in Aman and the investigations pursued throughout the following Ages. Their smiths and jewellers created objects whose renown extended far beyond the kingdoms where they were made, while their scholars contributed to the preservation of the languages and tales of ancient days. This tradition does not, however, mean that every Noldo possesses the knowledge of a great craftsman. Some devote themselves to music, the study of plants, navigation, or the service of their communities, while others have chiefly received military training. The qualities of their Race favour learning, but their actual mastery depends upon the disciplines to which they have devoted their lives.

The Sindar developed other traditions, deeply shaped by the kingdoms of Beleriand and the teachings preserved within the ancient Telerin communities. Their architecture, music, and arts bore witness, in particular, to the prosperity of Doriath and the relationships maintained with other peoples. The communities descended from the Nandor and the Silvan Elves, meanwhile, possess extensive knowledge of woodland materials, plants, and techniques suited to their environment. Forest dwellers can fashion weapons, tools, and instruments whose design meets the necessities of life among the trees, while travellers learn to employ available resources without compromising the safety of their communities. These skills are passed down by elders, but may also be enriched through contact with other peoples when craftsmen decide to share their knowledge.

Masters responsible for instruction occupy an important place in this transmission. Some teach the children of their community, while others welcome apprentices who have already devoted several decades to a discipline. Studies may concern languages, history, the properties of plants, construction, musical arts, or the knowledge necessary for travel. A scholar may preserve documents handed down from ancient kingdoms and compare them with his own memories, while a healer perfects his understanding of wounds and remedies. Workshops and places of learning thus foster enduring relationships between masters and pupils, particularly when several generations belong to the same professional tradition.

The knowledge of the Quendi must not, however, be regarded as universal. A craftsman who has devoted several centuries to making instruments may know nothing of the techniques required to build a fortress, while an experienced warrior may possess only limited knowledge of ancient languages. A Silvan Elf may accurately recognise the plants of his forest without knowing those of southern regions, while a Noldo trained in smithcraft must learn the customs of human communities before he can deal with their representatives. A long existence offers time to acquire knowledge, but does not impose any automatic accumulation of learning. The choice of a trade therefore forms an essential part of the character's history, particularly when he decides to begin a new apprenticeship or leave a community where his abilities are already recognised.

Languages, Song, and the Memory of Ancient Kingdoms

Languages occupy a fundamental place in the identity of the Quendi. Since their awakening at Cuiviénen, the Elves have developed tongues whose evolution bears witness to the migrations, separations, and encounters that have shaped their history. The Great Journey and the divisions between kindreds encouraged the emergence of distinct linguistic traditions, while exchanges between communities allowed certain more ancient elements to be preserved. Quenya remains particularly associated with scholarly traditions and the heritage of the Eldar who lived in Aman, while Sindarin gradually became the most widespread Elven language in north-western Middle-earth. Telerin, the tongues descended from Nandorin, and the various languages of the Avari belong to other branches of this heritage, whose use remains closely connected with the communities that preserved them.

Mastery of these languages depends upon education and personal history. A Noldo educated among ancient families may know Quenya and Sindarin, employing one for scholarly compositions and the other in everyday relationships. A Silvan Elf may speak a tongue particular to his community and possess only limited knowledge of the ancient languages of the West, while an Avar from the eastern regions may use linguistic forms unknown to the inhabitants of Lindon. Exchanges with Men and the Khazâd also lead some Quendi to learn their languages, particularly when they participate in trade, travel, or political alliances. A character may therefore possess great mastery of his own people's traditions while experiencing difficulty understanding the words of a companion belonging to another Elven Culture.

Song is one of the principal means of preserving memories. The Quendi compose tales devoted to their ancestors, the places they have inhabited, and the events that transformed their world. Some compositions preserve with great precision the words and deeds of figures long departed, while others recall landscapes, encounters, and the joys of a vanished age. Songs may be passed down over centuries and performed by artists who personally knew their composers, giving these works exceptional continuity. Instruments accompany celebrations, gatherings, and moments of rest, particularly when several generations come together and wish to share compositions associated with their family history.

Elven accounts nevertheless preserve different perspectives according to their peoples. A Noldo may recount the wars of Beleriand through the deeds of his sovereigns and the consequences of Fëanor's oath, while a Sinda recalls the events that befell Doriath and the families of its kingdom. A Silvan Elf may attach greater importance to the migrations of his ancestors and the history of the forests where his community settled, while an Avar possesses traditions of which western chroniclers know almost nothing. These memories may complement one another, but can also sustain disagreements, particularly when several peoples preserve different interpretations of an ancient event. A character may therefore know the tales of his Culture perfectly well without possessing equivalent knowledge of the whole of Elven history.

The Weight of Memories and the Perception of Time

Memory holds an essential place in the existence of the Quendi. Their longevity enables them personally to remember very ancient events, vanished places, and companions they encountered centuries earlier. An Elf may recall the construction of a dwelling that Men now regard as an ancient ruin, have known several sovereigns of a kingdom long vanished, or remember a forest before warfare transformed its territory. Where a human scholar must compare chronicles that sometimes contradict one another, certain Quendi possess direct testimony of the events under study. This memory encourages the remarkable transmission of knowledge, particularly when a master teaches his pupils a technique received several centuries earlier or when a singer performs a composition whose author he personally knew.

Yet such continuity may become painful. The wars against Morgoth, the ruin of Beleriand, the destruction of ancient kingdoms, and the loss of companions continue to affect those who experienced them. The passage of time does not always suffice to ease these losses, particularly when survivors encounter the remains of places where they once lived. Some Elves choose to preserve dwellings associated with their memories, while others prefer to leave lands where ancient events remain too vividly present. A character may have kept for centuries an object received from a departed friend, still remember the last words of a parent who fell in battle, or seek to understand the consequences of a decision made in his youth. Such memories may sustain his commitments, but also nourish guilt or attachment from which he finds it difficult to free himself.

Their perception of time therefore differs profoundly from that of mortal peoples. A project pursued over several decades may seem perfectly reasonable to them, particularly when it concerns the making of an object or the study of a discipline. A promise made to a Man may continue to bind them long after the passing of his descendants, while a political transformation that overturns a human generation may appear, in their eyes, as one episode among many others. This perspective may nourish patience, prudence, and a profound understanding of distant consequences, but may also lead some Elves to underestimate the urgency of human concerns. A character accustomed to waiting for the right moment may struggle to understand why his mortal companion wishes immediately to undertake a venture whose preparation might require several years.

Young Elves do not, however, necessarily share the solemnity of their elders. They discover their abilities, seek the company of their own kind, and experience a profound curiosity about lands they have never travelled. They may make mistakes, take rash decisions, or pursue ambitions whose dangers their parents already understand. Some elders welcome such aspirations with kindness, remembering their own youth, while others seek to protect their descendants from consequences they themselves endured. Relationships between generations can thus give rise to particularly enduring disagreements, especially when a young Elf wishes to leave a dwelling that his family has endeavoured to preserve for several centuries. A long life offers many opportunities to learn and change, but grants neither wisdom nor moderation from birth.

The Valar, the Arts, and the Powers of the World

The Quendi acknowledge Eru Ilúvatar as the Creator of all things and know of the existence of the Valar, the Powers who took part in the ordering of Arda. Their spiritual traditions differ profoundly from those of many human societies, particularly because some of their members have lived in Aman and personally known the Valar or the Maiar associated with their dwellings. Tales of ancient days therefore occupy a particular place in their understanding of the world, for they recount events of which some individuals still retain direct memories. Elven communities do not generally develop a permanent priesthood comparable to that of certain human religions. Their reverence for the Powers finds expression chiefly in songs, traditions, celebrations, and customs recalling their relationship with the world.

Varda holds an eminent place in their memory, for she is associated with the stars beneath which the first Quendi awoke. Her name, Elbereth, is invoked with profound reverence by many Elves, including communities whose ancestors never lived in Aman. Oromë remains associated with the memory of the first encounters between the Quendi and the Valar, as well as with the Great Journey. Yavanna occupies a particular place in traditions that attach great importance to trees and living beings, while Ulmo is closely associated with waters, rivers, and the history of peoples drawn towards the sea. These relationships vary according to Culture and personal experience. A Noldo who lived in Aman possesses knowledge of the Powers very different from that of an Avar whose ancestors refused Oromë's invitation.

The arts of the Elves maintain a distinctive relationship with the powers of the world. Certain songs possess a genuine influence upon their surroundings, while exceptional objects retain qualities their makers were able to impart to them. Healing, protection, and some works of craftsmanship may rest upon knowledge whose nature Men find difficult to understand, particularly when it was developed by masters who received the teachings of ancient days. This closeness between art, knowledge, and power does not, however, mean that every Elven creation is magical. An instrument may possess remarkable sound because of the skill of its maker, while a healer may achieve exceptional results through knowledge of plants and care without necessarily employing a magical discipline.

Magical traditions differ according to the peoples and the instruction received. The scholarly arts of the Noldor, the protective practices of certain woodland communities, and the knowledge inherited from ancient relationships with the Valar form bodies of learning whose methods and purposes are not identical. A character may devote several decades to studying one discipline without mastering those taught in another community, while an Elf possessing an exceptional talent for music may show no interest in the magical arts. In MERP-UI, these different paths find expression through the Cultures, Professions, and spell lists available to characters, in accordance with the principles of the RMU system. Membership of the Elven Race grants the natural qualities of the Quendi, but confers no automatic mastery of Essence, Mentalism, Channeling, or other magical disciplines.

Wars, Oaths, and Ancient Wounds

The history of the Elves is among the most glorious and tragic in Middle-earth. Their skill, endurance, and knowledge allowed the founding of remarkable kingdoms, but their divisions and ambitions also brought about catastrophes whose consequences endured across several Ages. During the First Age, the Noldor who returned from Aman established powerful kingdoms in Beleriand and continued their struggle against Morgoth, while the Sindar defended their own dwellings and other Elven communities were gradually drawn into the conflicts. The wars demanded considerable effort, mobilising craftsmen, guards, messengers, and families responsible for sustaining threatened settlements. Great battles brought about the destruction of cities, the scattering of populations, and the loss of countless companions whose memory the survivors preserved for a long time.

The military traditions of the Quendi reflect the diversity of their peoples. Some warriors fight in organised formations, protected by armour and shields of excellent quality, while others favour reconnaissance, ambushes, and the advantages of familiar terrain. Weapons employed include swords, spears, bows, and daggers, according to the knowledge and resources of each community. Companies charged with defending cities possess techniques different from those of woodland patrols, whose effectiveness depends greatly upon stealth and knowledge of the paths. The keen senses of the Elves and the precision of their movements favour such learning, but mastery requires training and experience that are not shared universally. A craftsman who has spent several centuries in a workshop may have received only elementary instruction in combat, while a guardian of the borders possesses skills developed through many years of vigilance.

Pride and rivalry among the Elves also contributed to their misfortunes. The oath of Fëanor and his sons bound them to a quest for the Silmarils whose consequences proved devastating, particularly when fidelity to their word led them to fight against other Eldar. The Kinslayings, the destruction of several kingdoms, and the divisions that afflicted their families recall how dangerous the determination to preserve a commitment may become when it refuses to acknowledge the consequences of its actions. Some of the greatest Elven lords displayed remarkable courage while committing errors that even their long lives could not undo. The memory of these events remains present in the traditions of the survivors, particularly when different lineages preserve opposing interpretations of the responsibilities involved.

During the Second Age, Sauron in turn exploited the ambitions and knowledge of certain Elven craftsmen. The events of Eregion and the making of the Rings of Power bear witness to the dangers that may arise from the desire to preserve the works and qualities of a world subject to change. Craftsmen who sought new knowledge and means of protecting their creations were confronted with the designs of an adversary capable of understanding their aspirations and turning them to his own advantage. The consequences of these undertakings extended into the Third Age, particularly within communities whose protection depended upon powers preserved by the ancient Elven Rings. The Quendi thus learned that their desire to preserve the world could become a weakness when it led them to seek means incompatible with the fate of the mortal lands.

The Elves Through the Ages

The history of the Quendi begins before the first rising of the Sun, with their awakening at Cuiviénen and the events that led to the Great Journey. During the First Age, the different Elven kindreds already possess distinct traditions, some profoundly transformed by their sojourn in Aman. The Noldor returning from the West found kingdoms in Beleriand, the Sindar defend their own dwellings, and other communities continue their history in the regions where they settled. The wars against Morgoth gradually overturn all these societies, bringing about the destruction of many settlements and the disappearance of distinguished lineages. A character of this period may belong to a family recently arrived from Aman, live among the inhabitants of Doriath, or grow up in a woodland community whose relationships with the great kingdoms remain limited. His education and the events he knows depend closely upon his people and the period chosen.

During the Second Age, survivors of the catastrophes of Beleriand develop new settlements in the western lands and renew their relationships with other peoples. Lindon becomes an important centre of Elven presence, while Eregion welcomes craftsmen whose knowledge contributes to the great achievements of the period. The woodland communities of the East continue their existence, sometimes under the rule of lords from other Elven kindreds, while exchanges with the Khazâd and Númenóreans encourage new alliances. Wars against Sauron nevertheless overturn these relationships, particularly when Eregion is destroyed and the Free Peoples must organise their resistance. A character may belong to the craftsmen of a prosperous city, participate in journeys between the kingdoms, or serve among the defenders of threatened settlements.

During the Third Age, the Elven communities of the West experience a gradual decline in population, while several of their great settlements remain centres of knowledge and protection. The inhabitants of Lindon, Rivendell, Lórien, and the Silvan realms pursue different purposes, but their activities contribute to preserving the lands surrounding them and the peoples who dwell there. Some Elves devote themselves to maintaining their homes and passing on knowledge, while others watch the borders, accompany travellers, or take part in wars against the servants of the Shadow. Their decisions are increasingly shaped by the prospect of departure into the West, particularly as Sauron's growing power again threatens the ancient kingdoms. The War of the Ring ultimately marks a decisive turning point, whose consequences concern not only the defeat of the Dark Lord but also the disappearance of the powers that had allowed certain Elven communities to preserve their dwellings.

During the Fourth Age, the presence of the Quendi in Middle-earth gradually becomes less conspicuous. Many Eldar depart for Aman, while the communities remaining in forests and valleys continue their existence in a world now dominated by Men. Ancient settlements change, certain commercial relationships evolve, and traditions whose preservation depended upon the great Elven kingdoms must find new means of transmission. This period offers particular possibilities for characters, especially when they wish to preserve a place, teach a skill, or accompany the transformation of a community to which they remain attached. Some choose to prepare their departure peacefully, while others continue their travels, work, or commitments, believing that their responsibilities in Middle-earth are not yet fulfilled.

Among the Other Peoples of Middle-earth

The relationships of the Quendi with Men occupy a singular place in their history. Since the alliances formed with the Edain during the First Age, some human families have maintained profound bonds with the Eldar, while other communities have never had direct dealings with them. The Dúnedain inherited some of the languages and knowledge received from their ancient allies, and their traditions preserve the memory of the services rendered by the great Elven lords. Yet this closeness remains marked by the difference between their destinies. An Elf may know several generations of the same human family and long preserve the memory of a companion whose descendants have forgotten his name. He may also find it difficult to understand the urgency with which a Man wishes to make a decision or accomplish an undertaking, particularly when the latter has only a few decades in which to realise his aspirations.

Relations with the Khazâd have known periods of mutual admiration and remarkable collaboration. The Noldor, in particular, recognised the exceptional qualities of Dwarven craftsmen, while certain Elven cities benefited from their techniques of construction and metallurgy. The collaborations between the inhabitants of Eregion and those of Khazad-dûm demonstrate the possibilities offered by such exchanges, especially when the two peoples shared a profound interest in materials and enduring works. Ancient quarrels and the tragic events of Beleriand nevertheless left considerable resentment, sometimes sustained by descendants who chiefly know the accounts preserved by their own families. A character may therefore greet a Dwarf with suspicion because of an ancient grievance, then discover during a shared undertaking qualities he gradually learns to respect.

The Hobbits remain little known to most Elven communities for many years. Those who live or travel in Eriador may nevertheless encounter them, particularly near the Shire and along the roads leading to the Grey Havens. Their small stature, attachment to domestic occupations, and manner of regarding the affairs of the world may surprise Elves whose concerns are bound to much older histories. Such differences may nevertheless encourage sincere relationships, particularly when the Quendi discover the depth of family attachments and the courage of which Hobbits are capable. An Elven character may thus learn to recognise the value of a life devoted to modest occupations, even when his own people attach great importance to works intended to endure across centuries.

Orcs, Trolls, and the other servants of Morgoth and later Sauron are among the most persistent adversaries of the Quendi. Their hostility dates back to the earliest conflicts of the world, and some Elves personally experienced wars whose consequences remain apparent several centuries later. The long memory of warriors may nourish understandable caution, particularly when the enemies they encounter recall ancient events. Relationships with other peoples nevertheless extend beyond inherited alliances and rivalries. Individuals respond differently to their history: some gladly seek the company of strangers, while others prefer to remain among their own kind. Ancient grievances may lead to the refusal of an alliance, but also to the desire to repair an injustice or renew relationships interrupted for several generations.

The Departure into the West and the Changing of the World

Since the end of the First Age, many Elves have left Middle-earth to reach Aman, while others have remained in the lands of their birth or among the communities they wished to preserve. The Grey Havens are among the principal places of departure into the West, where ships are prepared for those who decide to undertake the crossing. Travellers may arrive after years of preparation, bringing objects to which they are especially attached and memories of the dwellings they are leaving behind. Some families choose to depart together, while others are separated when their members make different decisions. Departure thus represents an important stage, particularly for Elves who have devoted much of their existence to protecting a territory or preserving an ancient settlement.

The desire to reach the West may arise gradually from weariness brought about by wars, losses, and the transformation of the world. An Elf may have seen several kingdoms vanish, witnessed the deaths of many companions, and found that the lands to which he remains attached have profoundly changed. The prospect of reaching Aman may then offer him the possibility of continuing his existence under different conditions, far from the conflicts and transformations that mark the mortal lands. Others nevertheless preserve a deep attachment to the forests, valleys, or dwellings where they were born and wish to continue caring for them. They may also feel responsible for communities to which they have devoted several centuries, particularly when their departure would leave companions without protection or interrupt instruction that is still needed.

At the end of the Third Age, the destruction of the One Ring also brings about the fading of the power of the Three Rings of the Elves. The realms that benefited from their influence can no longer preserve indefinitely the conditions that sustained their splendour, and the departure of the Eldar gathers pace. This transformation accompanies the establishment of the dominion of Men, whose kingdoms and settlements gradually assume a leading place in the fate of Middle-earth. The Quendi who remain in the mortal lands continue their existence in a world whose languages, institutions, and populations keep changing. Some choose to withdraw into distant regions, while others maintain relations with human communities and continue taking part in activities that help preserve the places to which they remain attached.

This fading does not transform every Elf into a melancholy being. Some continue their travels, teach their arts, raise children, maintain their homes, or seek new knowledge, while others prepare their departure with serenity. Awareness of the world's transformation may nourish sorrow, but may also encourage individuals to attach greater importance to the relationships and works they still wish to preserve. A character may therefore choose to remain in Middle-earth in order to fulfil a promise, protect a place, or pass on knowledge to those who will follow him. Departure into the West is a profound possibility within their existence, but personal circumstances determine when each individual chooses to undertake it.

Individual Will and the Weight of Ancient Loyalties

The Quendi possess freedom of choice comparable to that of the other Children of Ilúvatar, but the duration of their existence lends particular significance to their decisions. An oath sworn in youth may continue to bind them several centuries later, while an error committed during an ancient war may influence their relationships with other peoples for a long time. Such continuity encourages remarkable loyalty, particularly when individuals remain attached to their companions, families, or works to which they have devoted much of their lives. It may nevertheless nourish obstinacy when attachment to the past prevents recognition of the needs of the present.

Pride also holds an important place in certain Elven traditions. The great achievements of ancient kingdoms, accumulated knowledge, and relationships with the Valar may lead some characters to regard their people as superior to the other inhabitants of Middle-earth. Such a conviction may create difficulties with Men, the Khazâd, or Hobbits, particularly when their concerns appear modest beside Elven undertakings. Other Quendi have learned through their travels to recognise the value of mortal works and appreciate the qualities of companions whose lives remain brief. These differences of temperament reflect personal experiences and the teachings received, rather than an identical disposition among all members of the Race.

Ancient wounds may also exercise a profound influence. A character who witnessed the destruction of his home may seek to preserve the settlements that remain, while another wishes to recover objects or knowledge lost during the wars. Some remain attached to the oaths of their ancestors, particularly when they believe that faithfulness to one's word constitutes an obligation exceeding personal preference. Others instead seek to repair the consequences of ancient decisions, believing that the memory of their people should enable them to avoid new catastrophes. Such attitudes offer many possibilities for roleplaying, particularly when a character must choose between an ancient loyalty and relationships formed during his adventure.

The long existence of the Quendi also favours personal transformation. An Elf may have devoted several centuries to a discipline before discovering a new interest, moved to another dwelling after a catastrophe, or decided to resume an apprenticeship long abandoned. He may have experienced periods of prosperity and war, profound friendships, and painful separations, without these experiences entirely determining his future. Young and old alike remain capable of learning, experiencing new feelings, and changing their understanding of the world. Their history therefore offers considerable depth to characters, but should never confine them to an unchanging temperament.

Playing an Elf

Playing an Elf in Middle-earth means portraying a being whose relationship with time, memory, and other peoples differs profoundly from that of Men. His existence may continue across several Ages, but the knowledge he possesses depends upon his upbringing, the places where he has lived, and the experiences he has personally undergone. An Elf may belong to an ancient lineage whose tales reach back to Aman, have grown up in a city established after the destruction of Beleriand, or have been born in a woodland community whose traditions are almost unknown to the peoples of the West. His Race grants him remarkable qualities, but his Culture and personal history determine the languages he knows, the trades he has learned, and the relationships he maintains with the other inhabitants of Middle-earth.

A young Silvan Elf may have grown up in a woodland community, among families who have known the paths, streams, and resources of their territory for generations. He has learned to recognise animals, plants, and seasonal changes, gradually accompanying adults during the journeys and work necessary for communal life. He may have taken part in patrols charged with watching the paths, without yet encountering the dangers his masters faced during previous centuries. His departure may result from a mission entrusted to him by an elder, the disappearance of a companion, or the desire to discover lands beyond the forests. He may also wish to visit the ancient dwellings of the West, whose tales he knows but whose reality remains unfamiliar, and discover during his travels how greatly the customs of other Elven communities differ from those of his own family.

A Noldo may have devoted several decades to studying languages, making weapons, or learning an art passed down by his relatives. He knows the works of masters, some of whom lived in Aman, but his personal knowledge depends upon the disciplines he has chosen. He may undertake a journey to recover a manuscript, examine the remains of an ancient workshop, or seek the descendants of a craftsman whose teachings his family preserves. His history may also be marked by the consequences of an oath or ancient rivalry, particularly when his ancestors took part in the events that led the Noldor to return to Middle-earth. Such a character may feel great pride in his heritage while gradually discovering the mistakes made by earlier generations, and must decide whether he wishes to continue their commitments or repair their consequences.

A Sinda may belong to a family whose ancestors once lived in the kingdoms of Beleriand. He has received tales of Doriath, its rulers, and the events that brought about the disappearance of the ancient dwellings, particularly when some of his relatives still preserve personal memories of them. He may have learned the music, languages, and arts of his people, or received training intended to prepare him for service among the guards and counsellors of a lord. His adventure may be connected with the search for a vanished place, the preservation of a document, or service to a community that has maintained relationships with his family for many years. He may also wish to understand the choices made by ancient sovereigns, particularly when their decisions brought consequences whose weight their descendants still bear.

An Avar may belong to a community established in the eastern regions of Middle-earth, where his ancestors continued their history after refusing the Great Journey. He knows the traditions, languages, and customs of his people, but may be unfamiliar with much of the history that occupies a central place in the tales of the western Eldar. His journey westward may result from a migration, a commercial mission, or the desire to find other Elven communities of which he knows only a few names. The characters he encounters may regard his customs with curiosity, while he himself discovers peoples who attach particular importance to events of which his family preserves no memory. This difference allows him to approach Elven history from a distinct perspective, particularly when he must understand ancient rivalries between communities that nevertheless share a common origin.

An Elf belonging to the Vanyar presents more exceptional possibilities, particularly when a campaign takes place in Middle-earth. His history must correspond to the circumstances of the chosen Age and explain the reasons for his presence far from Aman, where his people chiefly remain. He may possess particular knowledge of traditions associated with the Valar, but does not thereby master every scholarly discipline of the Noldor or the customs of woodland communities. His arrival in the mortal lands may constitute a profoundly new experience, particularly when he discovers the consequences of wars, the fragility of kingdoms, and the concerns of peoples who have lived for centuries beyond the protection of the Powers of the West. Such an origin requires a sound historical justification and remains subject to the Gamemaster's approval.

The character's age is among the most important aspects of his conception. An Elf born during the Third Age has not personally experienced the wars of Beleriand, even if he has heard their tales since childhood and may have received instruction from masters who participated in them. A much older character may retain direct memories of these events, have known sovereigns whose names now belong to the chronicles, and still bear the consequences of decisions made several centuries earlier. Such antiquity must nevertheless remain consistent with the knowledge actually acquired. A craftsman may have devoted most of his life to perfecting a particular technique without possessing any military experience, while a warrior who has taken part in numerous campaigns may prove unskilled in negotiations or unfamiliar with the customs of recently encountered populations.

The personal motivations of the Quendi are numerous. A character may seek lost knowledge, find the descendants of an ancient companion, repair a wrong, protect a territory, or satisfy a curiosity long deferred. He may also wish to understand Men, discover the traditions of the Khazâd, or preserve relationships his family maintained with a foreign community. Some leave their homes to fulfil a commitment whose origins reach back several centuries, while others undertake journeys in search of a master capable of teaching them a new discipline. A young Elf may seek adventure out of a desire to discover unknown lands, whereas an elder may wish to revisit a place associated with personal memories and understand how it has changed.

Family relationships also provide an important source of roleplaying opportunities. A character may have grown up among relatives who personally experienced the great wars of ancient days and regard their decisions with respect, without necessarily sharing all their convictions. He may wish to continue a parent's work, preserve a dwelling, or fulfil a promise made before his birth. Departures into the West may also profoundly alter relationships between members of the same family, particularly when some wish to remain in Middle-earth while others believe their time there has come to an end. A character may thus devote part of his existence to preparing his own departure while maintaining commitments whose fulfilment still keeps him in the mortal lands.

The relationship with time should influence the character's decisions without imposing permanent slowness upon him. An Elf may show patience when undertaking a work intended to last several centuries, then act with great speed when he believes a situation demands an immediate decision. His longevity may encourage prudence, but also boldness when his experience enables him to recognise a particular opportunity. It may favour an understanding of distant consequences while sometimes making it difficult for him to appreciate the urgency of human concerns. A character may learn to respect the decisions of his mortal companions, even when they seem hasty to him, particularly when he understands that their lives leave them less time to accomplish their plans.

Memory may provide deeper motivations. An Elf may preserve the memory of a destroyed city and seek to recover works saved from its ruin, while another wishes to establish the precise circumstances of an event whose surviving accounts remain contradictory. A character may also bear responsibility for an ancient decision, particularly when he believes he contributed to a war or the destruction of a community. He may seek to repair the consequences of his actions, protect the descendants of those he could not save, or preserve knowledge whose loss would endanger the memory of his people. Such commitments give an adventure a significance that sometimes extends beyond immediate events, without preventing the character from forming new friendships and discovering personal reasons to continue his journey.

Relationships with other peoples offer numerous opportunities for growth. An Elf accustomed to the traditions of the West may discover, through a Dwarf, an understanding of craftsmanship founded upon knowledge he does not possess, while a character mistrustful of Men may learn to appreciate their courage and ability to accomplish great works during brief lives. Hobbits may reveal to him the value of an existence devoted to family relationships and ordinary occupations, particularly when he has long lived among communities concerned with ancient wars and great undertakings. These encounters may change his convictions, lead him to question certain prejudices, or strengthen loyalties whose value he now understands more fully.

The Professions available to the Quendi reflect the diversity of their traditions and knowledge. A Fighter may have received training among the forces charged with defending a city or the companies engaged in ancient wars, while a Ranger may possess extensive knowledge of the wild lands, animals, and paths used by travellers. A Rogue may have developed his skills during discreet missions, journeys, or negotiations requiring great caution, while a Bard may devote his life to preserving tales, studying languages, and maintaining the musical traditions of his people. Other Professions may be considered according to the chosen Culture and the compatibilities provided by MERP-UI. Access to magical disciplines remains subject to the teachings and restrictions defined by the RMU system, without the natural gifts of the Quendi or their longevity automatically granting mastery of spells.

The choice of Age is finally a decisive factor. During the First Age, a character may belong to the great communities of Beleriand, participate in migrations and wars, or live among the peoples who remained in the eastern regions. During the Second Age, he may experience the prosperity of settlements in Lindon and Eregion, exchanges with the Khazâd, or the wars against Sauron. During the Third Age, he may belong to the communities of Rivendell, Lórien, Lindon, or the Silvan realms, while the Fourth Age offers him the possibility of continuing his existence in a Middle-earth where Men now occupy a leading place. Each period lends a different significance to his ancestry, the events he personally remembers, and the reasons that may lead him to undertake a journey.

The Elves — Quendi Race is available in MERP-UI throughout the four Ages of Middle-earth, subject to the historical circumstances particular to each period. It represents the fundamental qualities shared by the Firstborn: their existence bound to Arda, their remarkable senses, endurance, lightness of movement, and nature free from human ageing. The choice of a Culture then determines the character's origins, kindred, upbringing, languages, traditions, and acquired skills. The Vanyar, Noldor, Teleri, Sindar, Nandor, Silvan Elves, Avari, and other communities developed in MERP possess distinct histories that influence their relationships and professional possibilities. Certain origins require particular justification according to the chosen Age, especially when a character belongs to a people chiefly established in Aman.

Exceptional unions between Elves and Men, and their descendants, the Peredhil, are represented separately among the Restricted Races of MERP-UI and are subject to particular conditions of character creation. Their history, the choices that may be granted to them, and the consequences of their mixed ancestry must therefore be distinguished from the nature of the Quendi.

Before approving the creation of an Elven character, the player and Gamemaster should determine his people of origin, family, the dwelling where he grew up, and the disciplines to which he has devoted his life. They should also establish his age, the events he personally experienced, and those he knows only through the tales of his community. His relationships with other peoples, attitude towards ancient traditions, and possible desire to depart into the West help define his personality, but his motivations must also belong to him. He may wish to preserve a dwelling, recover knowledge, fulfil a promise, repair a wrong, or discover lands his ancestors never travelled. The events of his adventure will allow him to weigh these aspirations against the commitments he has inherited and decide what he still wishes to accomplish in Middle-earth.

An Elf possesses an existence whose span exceeds that of kingdoms and human generations. He may preserve the memory of vanished lands, pursue works begun centuries earlier, and remain faithful to companions whose descendants have forgotten their names. This memory grants him particular knowledge and responsibilities, but the circumstances of his existence also allow him to discover, learn, and choose new paths. The bonds he decides to preserve, the works to which he devotes his time, and the commitments he accepts will determine the place he holds among the Quendi.
